title: Three times
hook: Peter denied Jesus three times; after the resurrection he is asked three times, lovest thou me? (John 21:15–17)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zacchaeus came down from the tree and gave back more than he took. Your line was fourfold. What did you repay? Today, a new week, and a friend who failed at the worst moment. Day nine hundred fifty-three.

I am not. Three short words, said in a courtyard at night, and it's cold. Servants and officers have made a fire of coals, and they're standing around it warming their hands. Peter is standing with them. Inside, Jesus has been arrested and is being questioned. A girl at the door looks at Peter and asks if he's one of this man's disciples. He says no. Then someone else asks. Then someone else. Three times, he says no. And then the rooster crows. Today: three times.
screen: `A FIRE OF COALS.` → `I AM NOT.` → `THREE TIMES, THEN THE ROOSTER.`

segments.voice: First, the failure. Peter isn't a stranger to Jesus. He's the one who said he would lay down his life for him. And when it counted, he warmed his hands by someone else's fire and said he didn't know him. Luke adds a detail that's hard to read: "the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter." And then: "Peter went out, and wept bitterly." No speech. Just a look, and a grown man crying outside. Second, the second fire. Turn to the end of John's Gospel. After the resurrection, some of the disciples have gone back to fishing. They come in at dawn and find Jesus on the shore, and John says: "they saw a fire of coals there." The same picture as the courtyard. A fire of coals. Breakfast is cooking on it. Third, the three questions. After they eat, Jesus turns to Peter: "Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me more than these?" Peter says: "Yea, Lord; thou knowest that I love thee." Jesus says, "Feed my lambs." Then he asks again. And a third time. John says Peter was grieved because he was asked the third time. Three denials, three questions. Every no in the courtyard gets a yes by the fire. Fourth, the job. Each time Peter answers, he gets work: feed my lambs, feed my sheep. Not probation. Not a lecture about the courtyard. Jesus doesn't mention the denial at all. He gives the man who failed the care of the others. Some Christians call this scene the restoring of Peter, and its shape is simple: the second chance comes with a real task, handed over by the fire.
screen: `DENIAL BY THE FIRE.` · `A SECOND FIRE OF COALS.` · `THREE TIMES: LOVEST THOU ME?` · `FEED MY SHEEP: A REAL TASK.` · then, large: `THOU KNOWEST THAT I LOVE THEE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath come and go. Think of someone who let you down and has been trying, in their own clumsy way, to come back. A friend who flaked. A sibling who said the wrong thing. A child, a parent, a colleague. Picture them by a small fire, asking if things can be all right. Now notice what you've been doing: keeping them at the door, or letting them in? Imagine giving them one real chance to make it right, a small task, a bit of trust. If the person who failed is you, picture being asked the question and answering yes. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Three times. Peter's three denials in the courtyard, and his three answers by a fire on the shore: thou knowest that I love thee. Today's word.
Your line: a second chance. Today, let someone who let you down make it right: give them one small, real way to do it, and let them. Day nine hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: In Christian teaching, John 21 is read as the restoring of Peter after his denial, and some preachers draw attention to the two fires of coals that frame the story.

fork.setup: you're Peter, eating breakfast on the shore with the one you denied three times. what does Jesus say to you?
options: he reminds you of the courtyard.
he tells you to go home.
fork.reveal: he asks three times, "lovest thou me?" and each yes is answered with a job: feed my lambs, feed my sheep.

trapdoor: what you thought: Peter got caught lying and felt bad.
what it means: three denials undone by three questions, and a second chance that comes with real work.

what a scholar hears: some readers notice John repeats one detail, a fire of coals in the courtyard and a fire of coals on the shore, so the restoring happens beside the same kind of fire as the failing.

notes: The hook follows John 18 (a damsel at the door, then others) and paraphrases; the first denial 'I am not' is John 18:17.

The fire of coals detail: John 18:18 and John 21:9 use the same Greek word (ἀνθρακιά); the voice says only that the picture is the same, from the KJV. Trapdoor floor 3 attributes the link to 'some readers'.
The well-known discussion of two Greek verbs for love (ἀγαπάω / φιλέω) in John 21:15–17 is left out on purpose; scholars differ on its weight.
'He said he would lay down his life for him' paraphrases John 13:37.
howItsDone: 'some preachers draw attention to the two fires' is a soft descriptive claim.
Luke 22:61–62 combined with John 21 across Gospels; the voice names each Gospel.
